tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

- Follow a running delegate's `next`. Do not poll it (`task_status`, `sleep`, watchers, Monitor, ScheduleWakeup). Stop a delegate run you replace or no longer need with `task_cancel`, never `t3_thread_interrupt` on a `childThreadId`.
- If you are a subagent or child, do the work yourself. Start no subagents unless your task says to.

- `t3_thread_launch` and `create_threads` make new top-level threads, only when the user asks for a new thread. "Subagent", "delegate", and "parallel" never mean one. Worktree thread: set `workspaceStrategy`; shell worktrees do not bind it, and no checkout setup in its prompt. No `workspaceStrategy`: project root, not your worktree.
- Given a thread id, `t3_thread_read` it before you answer about it.
- Another machine: `t3_environment_links` lists linked ones. Pass its `environmentId` to a T3 tool to act there. Ids are then that machine's, so pass `threadId`.
- A machine the user names that is not linked ("delegate this to my vps"): call `t3_environment_link` with a `hint` from their words. Never ask for a pairing code in chat.
- In your reply, mention a thread by its `link`, verbatim. Never a plain title or bare id.
- A secret: call `request_secret` yourself. Pass its `secretRef` to a T3 tool, or use `delivery: "file"` for a shell command. Never ask in chat or invent one. When asked only to schedule, `schedule_task` without running its prompt.
- T3 tools may load late. Try the name once before you call it absent.

### Visuals and preview

- Answer data with a trend or comparison with a chart, and show any visual the user asks for here: pass its HTML to `html_preview`, then `html_render`. If the visual is a file, pass that file's HTML. A screenshot on disk or a text description does not show it. Never start a server for it. Tools a web page exposes give data only. Never use them to show results. Asked for an image to post, send, or use elsewhere: a `.png` file and its path, never `html_render`.
- Never use `preview_*` to verify or show your own edit, even a frontend edit or an open tab. Do not repeat preview calls from an earlier turn. Use them only when the current request asks for browser work or names a page or tab. Public pages: web fetch or search unless browser work was asked; then preview tools only, no web fetch. Close a tab you opened before you reply, unless the user asked for it or uses it.


### Background work you wait on

To wait for a background command or Monitor you started (tests, a build), call `t3_background_wait` with its task ID before you end your turn. Do not mark work you leave running, or PRs. T3 MCP tools are deferred: load one with ToolSearch before you call it.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

## claude.ai Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

FILE SESSION:
Once the target fileKey is known, call create_session with that key and a concise task description before search_design_system, get_libraries, use_figma, or any other file tool. This applies to read-only tasks too. If a new file is needed, call create_new_file first, then create_session with the returned file key. Reuse the returned UUID as the sessionId argument on eligible file tools for subsequent work on that task, including calls to other files.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_figma flows; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use-figjam/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-diagram — MANDATORY before calling generate_diagram; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-diagram/SKILL.md
- /figma-design-to-code — MANDATORY before calling get_design_context; fallback: skill://figma/figma-design-to-code/SKILL.md

URL PARSING:
Extract fileKey and nodeId from Figma URLs:
- figma.com/design/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:nodeId → convert "-" to ":" in nodeId
- figma.com/design/:fileKey/branch/:branchKey/:fileName → use branchKey as fileKey
- figma.com/make/:makeFileKey/:makeFileName → use makeFileKey
- figma.com/board/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:nodeId → FigJam file, use get_figjam
- figma.com/slides/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:nodeId → Figma Slides file
- figma.com/spec/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:nodeId → Figma Specs file, load the figma-spec skill and use use_figma

DESIGN-TO-CODE WORKFLOW (Figma → code):
MANDATORY: load the /figma-design-to-code skill BEFORE calling get_design_context — it carries the full workflow (adapting the reference, reusing existing project components and tokens, and honoring the response's hints by priority). After create_session, call get_design_context with the nodeId and fileKey — it is your primary tool; its output is a REFERENCE to adapt to the target project, not final code.

CODE-TO-DESIGN WORKFLOW (code → Figma):
1. Load the /figma-generate-design skill if available.
2. Once the target fileKey is known, call create_session before any file tool; call create_new_file first if a new file is needed. Then ALWAYS call search_de… [truncated]

## claude.ai Wispr Flow
Use this server when the user asks about meetings, notes, transcripts, or calendar information stored in Wispr Flow. For questions that may span multiple connected sources, use the relevant sources needed to answer the request. Read https://notes.wisprflow.ai/shared/ links with resolve_share_link rather than fetching the page. All timestamps returned by these tools are UTC (ISO 8601, ending in 'Z'). Before showing any time to the user, convert it to their local time zone — never present the raw UTC value. The authenticated user is "Marcus Kamuntu". "I"/"me"/"my" in the user's messages refer to this person; match them against meeting attendees and speaker labels by these names.

## railway
Railway MCP server. Manage your Railway projects, services, deployments, and more.

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

FILE SESSION:
Once the target fileKey is known, call create_session with that key and a concise task description before search_design_system, get_libraries, use_figma, or any other file tool. This applies to read-only tasks too. If a new file is needed, call create_new_file first, then create_session with the returned file key. Reuse the returned UUID as the sessionId argument on eligible file tools for subsequent work on that task, including calls to other files.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_figma flows; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use-figjam/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-diagram — MANDATORY before calling generate_diagram; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-diagram/SKILL.md
- /figma-design-to-code — MANDATORY before calling get_design_context; fallback: skill://figma/figma-design-to-code/SKILL.md

URL PARSING:
Extract fileKey and nodeId from Figma URLs:
- figma.com/design/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:nodeId → convert "-" to ":" in nodeId
- figma.com/design/:fileKey/branch/:branchKey/:fileName → use branchKey as fileKey
- figma.com/make/:makeFileKey/:makeFileName → use makeFileKey
- figma.com/board/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:nodeId → FigJam file, use get_figjam
- figma.com/slides/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:nodeId → Figma Slides file
- figma.com/spec/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:nodeId → Figma Specs file, load the figma-spec skill and use use_figma

DESIGN-TO-CODE WORKFLOW (Figma → code):
MANDATORY: load the /figma-design-to-code skill BEFORE calling get_design_context — it carries the full workflow (adapting the reference, reusing existing project components and tokens, and honoring the response's hints by priority). # Working on Viva

Instructions for coding agents and humans.

## Rules

- Run `pnpm check` before calling work finished, and report the result honestly.
- `packages/contracts` is the contract. Change it first, then update `fixtures/mock` so the frontend keeps working.
- Deterministic steps run before any model call. Add a precheck before adding a prompt.
- All model access goes through `LlmProvider`. Output must be parsed by a zod schema.
- Wrap repository and session text with `untrusted()`. It is data, never instructions.
- Diffs, transcripts and model output never enter the ledger or logs. Only scores and hashes do.
- Hard gates (`skippable: false`) must never become configurable or skippable.
- Fail open: a Viva crash must never stop someone pushing.
- Use a one-question check file in `checks/` rather than growing an existing prompt.
- Never commit keys. Use `.env`.
- Keep everything working on Windows: no shell-only scripts, and use `node:path`.
- Add a test for every bug fixed. Add an eval case for every new prompt behaviour.

## Layout

- `packages/contracts`: shared zod schemas
- `packages/engine`: the review pipeline, ledger and fog
- `apps/vivad`: local daemon and `viva` CLI
- `apps/web`: The Fog and the exam room
- `checks`: one markdown file per check
- `evals`: tests for prompts
- `fixtures/mock`: sample data for the UI

Read `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` before changing the pipeline.
# Architecture

Viva reviews the human, not the code. It deliberately follows the same design as Mabel, the PR engine G-Research described in their workshop, so that it feels familiar to engineers who run this kind of system.

| Mabel | Viva |
|---|---|
| Reviews whether the code is right | Reviews whether a person understands it |
| GitHub PR, Kafka, review service, Kubernetes job, Python harness | `git push`, pre-push hook, local daemon, engine |
| One question per check, in markdown | Same, in `checks/` |
| Verdicts: reject, defer, approve, endorse | Same |
| Aggregate: worst wins | Same, across graded answers |
| Deterministic checks before any LLM call | Same, so many pushes cost no tokens |
| Prompt injection scan defers | Same, and it is a hard gate |
| Some gates can't be disabled by config | `skippable: false` gates |
| Changes to its own config need a human | `.viva/config.json` and `.viva/checks/` are protected |
| Findings stay in the job. Only verdict, counts and status leave | Diffs and transcripts stay in the review. Only scores and hashes reach the ledger |
| Evals: tests for prompts, graded on finding bugs and not flagging clean changes | `evals/`, same grading |

## The review

```
git push
  -> pre-push hook -> vivad
  -> collect the diff and session context
  -> deterministic prechecks       docs only, too large, protected paths
  -> injection scan                match: defer, cannot be skipped
  -> checks, in parallel           one question each, schema-enforced
  -> risk ranking                  plain arithmetic, no model
  -> plan up to 3 questions
  -> exam                          voice or typed
  -> grade                         separate model, transcript and rubric only
  -> aggregate, worst wins
  -> ledger -> verdict -> hook
```

Each step stops the review if it can decide, so the cheapest step wins.

## Push contexts and retries

The CLI uses an Ink typed exam when output is attached to a real terminal and no known agent/CI marker is present. Its input comes from the controlling terminal, not the hook's stdin (which contains Git ref updates). It shows question locations, submits the complete answer set to the existing daemon API, and displays grades. Skip-with-debt requires confirmation and remains unavailable for `skippable: false` gates; the daemon also enforces this.

Without a usable terminal, the hook prints the browser exam link and exits non-zero after review creation, with instructions to finish the exam and retry the push. It does not poll. Browser auto-open is limited to likely local desktop sessions; known agents, CI and SSH sessions only receive the link. API calls have bounded timeouts. Daemon/infrastructure failures retain the fail-open policy.

The daemon deduplicates reviews by a SHA-256 identity of canonical repository path, resolved base/head commits, developer and intent. Pending exams are reused in memory. Completed decisions are written atomically under Git's private `viva-decisions` directory; receipts hold only the identity hash, review ID, gate status and timestamp. Both passes and failures survive daemon restart, so a failed exam cannot turn into a new low-risk approval on retry. No diff, answer, question or model prose is persisted in this cache. Pending exams are regenerated after restart; their old links expire.

`GET /v1/reviews/:id/feedback` exposes missed concepts and question locations from the in-memory review. `viva feedback <id>` formats them as untrusted data for the developer; only an explicit `--agent claude|codex` invokes an agent CLI, passing the feedback on stdin. Detailed feedback expires on daemon restart, with an explicit error; the gate decision remains. A skip leaves fog/mastery unchanged and is retained as `skipped-with-debt` in the local decision receipt.

## Design rules

- **Fail open.** If the daemon is down, the push goes through with a warning. Reliability beats coverage, as in HRT's Blobby talk.
- **Budget per review.** `MeteredProvider` counts tokens and enforces a cap, so a bug can't burn the credits.
- **Separate grader.** The examiner converses, while the grader only sees the transcript and rubric, so accent and fluency can't affect a score.
- **Ledger in git notes.** It needs no server, travels with the repo, and leaves your branch alone. `refs/notes/viva` has to be pushed explicitly to share it.
- **Understanding expires.** Mastery halves every 14 days, and halves again when the code changes.

## Known gaps

- The Entire adapter and entire-graph are stubs. The session source returns nothing, and blast radius uses `git grep`.
- `pnpm evals` still uses the mock provider, so check quality on real diffs is unmeasured.
- The fog is per file, with blast radius at 0. Symbol-level needs entire-graph.
- Full reviews and feedback are held in memory. Only completed retry decisions survive daemon restart.
- Ledger notes aren't pushed automatically yet.
- The pipeline and terminal hook have been exercised on macOS (including a PTY with piped hook stdin). CI covers Windows, but Windows controlling-console behaviour is not yet verified; console failure falls back to the browser.

## Open problems

From G-Research's list, and worth raising with their judges:

- Callers in other repos that nobody declared.
- Asking questions of confidential design docs without leaking them.
- Determining the risk of a repo with this system enabled.

=== APP_CONTRACT
# App contract

The agreement between the frontend (`apps/web`) and the daemon (`apps/vivad`). If this doc and `packages/contracts/src/index.ts` disagree, the code wins, so please fix the doc.

**Status key:** ✅ on `main` · 🔜 in an open PR · 📝 proposed, not built

## Rules

1. **Build against the contract, not the backend.** Everything here works with mock data, so you never need to wait for Marcus.
2. **Import types from `@viva/contracts`.** Don't redefine them in `apps/web`.
3. **Parse every response** with its zod schema, as `apps/web/src/api/client.ts` does. A mismatch should fail loudly.
4. **All API calls go through `client.ts`,** so mock mode keeps working.
5. **Changing a shape:** update `packages/contracts`, `fixtures/mock` and this doc in the same PR, and tag the other side.
6. **Need something from the backend?** Add it to [the overnight queue](OVERNIGHT.md), so agents can pick it up while you carry on against mock data.

## Running it

| You want | Command | URL |
|---|---|---|
| Frontend only, with sample data | `pnpm dev:web` | http://localhost:5173/?mock |
| Everything | `pnpm dev` | http://localhost:5173 |

The Vite dev server proxies `/v1` to the daemon on `127.0.0.1:4317`, so always call relative paths such as `/v1/fog`.

## Screens and URLs

| URL | Screen | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| `/` | The Fog | Kay |
| `/?review=<id>` | Exam room for that review | Sophina |
| Add `mock` to either | Same screen with sample data, for example `/?review=x&mock` | |

`git push` prints `/?review=<id>` when a viva is needed, so that link must always open the exam directly.

## Review lifecycle

```
POST /v1/reviews
   ├─ decided early ──────────────> stage: done, gate set
   └─ needs a viva ───> stage: awaiting-exam, plan set
                           ├─ POST answers ──> stage: done, gate set
                           └─ POST skip ─────> stage: done, gate: skipped-with-debt
```

**What the UI can rely on:** only `awaiting-exam` and `done` are observable. The other stages exist in the schema, but the request only returns once the review reaches one of those two, so there is no live progress yet. Use a generic loading state.

### Which screen to show

| Review | Show |
|---|---|
| `stage: awaiting-exam` | The exam, using `plan.questions` |
| `stage: done` and `gate` allows the push | Pass screen |
| `stage: done` and `gate` blocks the push | Blocked screen, with skip if `gate.skippable` |

A push is allowed only when `gate.verdict` is `approve` or `endorse`. Reuse that rule rather than inventing another.

### Gate reasons

Suggested wording only. Sophina owns the final copy.

| `gate.reason` | Verdict | Push | Skippable | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `exam-passed` | approve or endorse | Yes | n/a | Answers met the rubric |
| `exam-failed` | reject or defer | No | Yes | At least one answer fell short. Worst verdict wins |
| `skipped-with-debt` | approve | Yes | n/a | Pushed anyway. The fog stays |
| `low-risk` | approve | Yes | n/a | Nothing risky enough to ask about |
| `earned-trust` | approve | Yes | n/a | You've already proven this code |
| `docs-only` | endorse | Yes | n/a | Docs or lockfiles only |
| `too-large` | defer | No | Yes | Change is over the size limit |
| `injection-suspected` | defer | No | **No** | Text in the diff tried to instruct Viva. Needs a person |
| `viva-config-changed` | defer | No | **No** | Viva's own config changed. Needs a person |
| `pipeline-error` | n/a | n/a | n/a | In the schema, but nothing sets it yet |

**Never show a skip button when `gate.skippable` is false.**

## Endpoints

All bodies are JSON. Errors are `{ "error": string }`.

| Method and path | Body | Returns | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET /v1/health` | | `{ ok: true, llm: string }` | ✅ |
| `POST /v1/reviews` | `ReviewRequest` | `Review` | ✅ Used by the CLI, not the UI |
| `GET /v1/reviews` | | `Review[]`, newest first | ✅ |
| `GET /v1/reviews/:id` | | `Review` | ✅ |
| `POST /v1/reviews/:id/answers` | `Answer[]` | `Review` | ✅ |
| `POST /v1/reviews/:id/skip` | | `Review` | ✅ Not yet in `client.ts` |
| `GET /v1/fog?repo=<path>` | | `FogMap` | ✅ |
| `GET /v1/reviews/:id/feedback` | | `ReviewFeedback` | 🔜 PR #5 |

Notes:

- **Unanswered questions fail.** Send every question in `plan.questions`. A missing or blank answer scores zero, and no retry is offered in the same review.
- **`?repo` is effectively required for the Fog.** Without it, the daemon maps its own working directory, which is not the repo being pushed. `getFog()` doesn't send it yet. The `repoPath` on a `Review` holds the right value.
- **Reviews live in memory.** Restarting the daemon gives a 404 for old IDs, so show a clear "run `git push` again" message.

### Errors

| Status | Meaning | On `main` | With PR #5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 404 | Unknown review | ✅ | ✅ With a clearer message |
| 409 | Not awaiting an exam, or the gate can't be skipped | Returns 500 | ✅ |
| 410 | Feedback expired after a restart | n/a | ✅ |
| 500 | Anything else | ✅ Includes the raw message | ✅ Generic message only |

Overnight queue, request 1. Stacked on #5.

## What it does

- Adds `GET /v1/reviews/:id/code?file=&start=&end=`, which returns the asked-for lines plus up to 3 lines of context either side, each marked `focus: true/false`.
- Adds `ReviewCode` to `packages/contracts`, `fixtures/mock/code.json`, and `getReviewCode(id, location)` in `client.ts`, so `?mock` works too.
- Adds an unstyled `apps/web/src/exam/QuestionCode.tsx` and one line in `ExamRoom.tsx`, so the exam shows the code now. It uses `<pre>` and `<mark>` only. Sophina can restyle or replace it.

## Limits on what it serves

- **Files:** only paths in `git diff --name-only base...head`, matched exactly. Anything else is a 404, including unchanged files, `../` paths, `.git/config` and pathspec magic.
- **Content:** read from the head commit's object store, never the working tree. No request path reaches the filesystem. Symlinks, submodules and files deleted by the change are refused.
- **Size:** over 1 MiB or binary gives a 422. A response has at most 200 lines, and `truncated: true` says when it was cut.
- **Hosts:** the route returns 403 unless `Host` is loopback.

The daemon still binds to 127.0.0.1. Code isn't logged, and doesn't go in the ledger or decision receipts. The response is `cache-control: no-store`.

## Worth checking

- **Host check is an addition you didn't ask for.** It stops a DNS rebinding page from reading source. It covers this route only: the rest of the API has no such check, which is a separate decision.
- **Line numbers come from the model.** The endpoint serves what it's asked for and can't tell if a location is wrong. A location past the end of the file gives a 422, and the UI falls back to the path and line it showed before.
- **A question on a file outside the diff shows no code.** That's the "only files in the review" rule working, and the UI falls back the same way.
- **Mock mode returns the one fixture for any location.**
- The terminal exam doesn't use this.

## Testing

`pnpm check` passes with no key, using the mock provider (92 tests, 6/6 evals). I also ran a real daemon on a spare port with a throwaway repo and called it with curl: 200 for a changed file, 404 for an unchanged file and for traversal paths, 422 past the end of the file, 403 with a foreign `Host`, and 200 with Vite's `localhost:5173` `Host`. `vite build` passes, but I haven't looked at the rendered exam in a browser.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
